Part 1 of 9

A Rising or a Setting Sun?

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 1: How can the American constitutional framework adapt to the strategic challenges of the twenty-first century while maintaining institutional legitimacy?

FQ 6: Identify the ways in which the Constitution remains a living document capable of managing twenty-first century conflicts, explaining how the Framers' design of institutional friction and adaptability has enabled the republic to survive previous periods of acute stress.

IN MY WORDS: Franklin wondered if the Constitution’s sun was rising or setting. What would you say about it today?

Reading AFranklin’s Sun

On September 17, 1787, the final day of the Constitutional Convention, Benjamin Franklin rose to address the assembled delegates. He acknowledged that the document they had produced was not perfect, that there were provisions he objected to, but he stated that he would support it because he despaired of the possibility of any assembly producing a better one.

Franklin then offered a reflection that has resonated across the centuries: looking at the half-sun carved on the back of George Washington’s chair, which he had contemplated throughout the long summer of debate, he said he had often wondered whether it was a rising or a setting sun. “Now at length,” he concluded, “I have the happiness to know that it is a rising, and not a setting, sun.”

Two and a half centuries later, the question Franklin posed is being asked again, with new urgency and new complexity.

Word help: delegates = people sent to a meeting to speak for others · acknowledged = admitted · provisions = parts of a document · despaired = lost hope · resonated = kept echoing · urgency = a need to act quickly

Chapter 20, Introduction.

Source AFranklin and the Rising Sun

Benjamin Franklin made this closing remark at the Constitutional Convention in September 1787, as recorded by James Madison in his notes. This is a primary source, and it is in the public domain.

“at the back of which a rising sun happened to be painted”
“it is a rising and not a setting Sun.”

Word help: painted = drawn with paint · rising sun = a sun coming up at the start of a new day · setting sun = a sun going down at the end of the day · delegates = people chosen to speak for others · convention = a formal meeting

Benjamin Franklin, closing remark, Federal Convention, Sept. 17, 1787, in Madison’s notes, Gordon Lloyd, ed., Debates in the Federal Convention of 1787 (Ashbrook Center, 2014). Quotations checked at teachingamericanhistory.org/document/benjamin-franklins-speech-federal-convention/. Primary source.

Source question. Use Source A and Reading A. What was Franklin asking about the new Constitution, and what picture did he use to ask it?

Reading BA Document That Kept Going

The constitutional framework that emerged from Philadelphia in 1787 has survived a civil war, two world wars, the Great Depression, the internal upheavals of Reconstruction and the civil rights era, and the Cold War’s constant threat of nuclear annihilation.

It has expanded the boundaries of citizenship from a narrow class of propertied white men to include all Americans regardless of race, gender, or economic status. It has presided over the transformation of the United States from a coastal agricultural republic of four million people into the world’s most powerful and technologically sophisticated democracy of more than three hundred million.

By any historical measure, the American constitutional design has proved extraordinarily resilient and remarkably adaptable.

Word help: framework = the basic structure · upheavals = big, disruptive changes · annihilation = total destruction · propertied = owning land or other property · sophisticated = advanced · resilient = able to recover from trouble · adaptable = able to change when needed

Chapter 20, Introduction.

Reading CNew Stresses

But resilience is not invulnerability, and adaptability requires active effort rather than automatic adjustment. The specific challenges confronting the American republic at the opening of the third decade of the twenty-first century are, in several respects, qualitatively different from those the framework has previously managed.

Political polarization has reached levels that were not considered sustainable by previous generations of political scientists, producing legislative dysfunction and eroding the social trust that democratic governance requires. Artificial intelligence and algorithmic governance are introducing forms of administrative decision-making that the protections of due process, equal protection, and the separation of powers were not designed to address.

The deliberate production and distribution of digital disinformation has put the quality of democratic deliberation under sustained attack. And the emergence of cyberspace as a new domain of state competition and conflict, which includes cyber warfare, has created vulnerabilities in voting systems, critical government networks, and the information environment that citizens depend on to make informed choices.

The chapter does not promise final answers. Its aim is to give students the conceptual tools to judge reform proposals on their merits and to tell changes that would improve democracy from those that would merely help one political faction.

Word help: invulnerability = being impossible to harm · qualitatively different = different in kind, not just amount · political polarization = a growing gap between the two parties · dysfunction = not working well · cyber warfare = digital attacks meant to disrupt a country’s systems · merits = real strengths and weaknesses

Part 2 of 9

Madison’s Machine and the Map

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 2: Analyze the root causes of modern political polarization — including gerrymandering, media echo chambers, and negative partisanship — and explain how hyper-partisanship has transformed the constitutional design of separated powers from a mechanism of productive compromise into one of near-total obstruction.

IN MY WORDS: Why did the Framers expect leaders to compromise, and how do district maps change that?

Reading DMadison’s Machine and Hyper-partisanship

James Madison’s constitutional design rested on a carefully reasoned theory of how institutions could channel the inevitable conflict of political factions into productive outcomes. By separating the powers of government among three branches, requiring broad coalitions to enact significant legislation, and creating multiple points at which any single faction could be checked, Madison believed he had designed a system in which “ambition must be made to counteract ambition.”

The design assumed that political actors with different interests and constituencies would need to compromise to govern. What Madison did not fully anticipate was that the two major parties would sort themselves into such ideologically homogeneous and mutually hostile camps that compromise itself became politically unacceptable.

The modern condition of hyper-partisanship, in which the parties are organized around fundamentally incompatible worldviews and motivated primarily by negative partisanship, has not eliminated the system’s friction, but it has transformed that friction from a mechanism of productive compromise into a mechanism of pure obstruction.

Word help: factions = groups with shared political interests · channel = guide · counteract = work against · homogeneous = all alike · hyper-partisanship = fierce party loyalty and hostility that blocks compromise · obstruction = blocking progress

Chapter 20, Section I, “The Polarization Crisis and Legislative Gridlock.”

Write the letter of the best answer, then explain in one sentence how the reading shows it.

Reading EGerrymandering

The process of drawing congressional and state legislative district boundaries, redistricting, which occurs after each decennial census, has become one of the most consequential exercises in political manipulation in American democracy.

Gerrymandering, the drawing of district boundaries to advantage a particular party or protect incumbent officeholders, is as old as the republic itself. The term derives from a salamander-shaped district created by Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry in 1812. But highly granular voter data and sophisticated mapping software have made it dramatically more precise and effective in the modern era than at any previous point in American history.

Word help: redistricting = redrawing election district lines · decennial census = the population count every ten years · consequential = having big effects · incumbent = a person already holding an office · granular = very detailed · manipulation = shaping something for your own benefit

Chapter 20, Section I, “Gerrymandering and the Architecture of Polarization.”

Reading FSafe Seats and Primary Elections

The mechanism through which partisan gerrymandering contributes to polarization operates at the level of the primary election. In a district drawn to be safely Republican or safely Democratic, in which one party is guaranteed to win the general election regardless of which candidate it nominates, the only competitive election is the party primary.

Primary electorates are typically more ideologically extreme than general election electorates: the voters who participate in low-turnout primaries tend to be more intensely partisan, more ideologically consistent, and more hostile to compromise. In a safe district, a Republican member of Congress who cooperates with Democrats faces a primary challenge from their right; a Democratic member who compromises faces a primary challenge from their left.

The incentive structure of the safe district therefore systematically punishes the behavior, cross-party cooperation and legislative compromise, that the Madisonian system was designed to encourage.

Word help: primary election = a vote within one party to pick its candidate · general election = the final election between parties · electorate = the people who vote · ideologically extreme = holding very strong, one-sided political beliefs · incentive = a reward or penalty that shapes behavior · systematically = in a regular, built-in way

Chapter 20, Section I, “Gerrymandering and the Architecture of Polarization.”

Reading GThe Court Steps Back: Rucho v. Common Cause

The Supreme Court has addressed the constitutionality of partisan gerrymandering and reached a conclusion that has effectively removed federal judicial oversight from the practice. In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), Chief Justice Roberts’s majority opinion held that partisan gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond the reach of federal courts: while extreme partisan gerrymanders may be “unjust,” the Constitution does not provide federal courts with a workable standard for adjudicating them.

This ruling left the remedy exclusively in the hands of state courts interpreting state constitutional provisions, Congress, which could regulate redistricting by statute, or the political process itself, including the growing number of states that have adopted independent redistricting commissions to remove the line-drawing authority from partisan legislators.

Word help: oversight = watching and checking · political question = an issue the courts say belongs to the elected branches · adjudicating = deciding in court · workable standard = a clear rule judges can apply · statute = a law passed by a legislature · independent commission = a group that is not run by the political parties

Chapter 20, Section I, “Gerrymandering and the Architecture of Polarization.”

Source BThe Court on Gerrymandering

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote these words for the Court in 2019. They come from the opinion in Rucho v. Common Cause. This is a primary source, and Supreme Court opinions are in the public domain.

“We conclude that partisan gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond the reach of the federal courts.”
“Excessive partisanship in districting leads to results that reasonably seem unjust.”
“One way they are doing so is by placing power to draw electoral districts in the hands of independent commissions.”

Word help: conclude = decide after thinking · political questions = issues for elected leaders, not judges · excessive = too much · districting = drawing election districts · reasonably = in a way that makes sense · independent commissions = groups set up apart from the parties

Rucho v. Common Cause, 588 U.S. ___ (2019), opinion of the Court (Roberts, C.J.). Quotations checked at law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/18-422. Primary source.

Part 3 of 9

Echo Chambers, Hostility, and Stress

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 2: Analyze the root causes of modern political polarization — including gerrymandering, media echo chambers, and negative partisanship — and explain how hyper-partisanship has transformed the constitutional design of separated powers from a mechanism of productive compromise into one of near-total obstruction.

FQ 4: Assess the impact of digital disinformation on the marketplace of ideas and the formation of public opinion, explaining how the deliberate spread of false information threatens institutional legitimacy and the quality of democratic self-governance.

IN MY WORDS: How do news habits, party hostility, and Senate rules add to polarization, and has the country survived it before?

Reading HEcho Chambers and Negative Partisanship

Gerrymandering restructures the incentives that elected officials face; media fragmentation and algorithmic curation restructure the informational environment in which citizens form their political identities. As Chapter 15 examined, the shift from a broadcasting landscape, in which a few organizations delivered a common factual reference to a mass national audience, to a narrowcasting landscape of algorithmically curated ideological enclaves has produced an electorate divided not just in its policy preferences but in its basic understanding of shared political reality.

The result is a reinforcement of what political scientists call negative partisanship: voters are motivated less by positive identification with their own party and its agenda than by hostility and fear directed at the opposing party. Research by political scientists such as Alan Abramowitz has documented a shift over the past three decades. As recently as the 1990s, most voters could give a positive policy reason for their party identification; today, many partisan voters are primarily motivated by the belief that the other party is a genuine threat to the country.

Word help: echo chamber = a place where you hear mostly your own views repeated · fragmentation = breaking into separate pieces · narrowcasting = sending messages to small, targeted groups · enclaves = separate groups · negative partisanship = voting mainly out of dislike for the other party · rationale = reason

Chapter 20, Section I, “Media Echo Chambers, Negative Partisanship, and the Erosion of Democratic Trust.”

Visual CParty Hostility

Reading IWhy Negative Partisanship Hurts the Design

Negative partisanship has several consequences that are specifically damaging to the Madisonian constitutional design. It makes compromise across party lines politically toxic, because cooperation with the enemy party is experienced by the partisan base not as statesmanship but as betrayal.

It makes losing a political contest feel not like normal democratic competition but like an existential threat, raising the political stakes of every election to levels that can encourage extraordinary measures to prevent defeat.

And it erodes the basic social trust, the acceptance that political opponents are legitimate competitors rather than enemies to be defeated by any available means, that functional democratic governance requires.

Word help: toxic = poisonous or harmful · statesmanship = wise leadership for the whole country · betrayal = disloyalty to your own side · existential threat = a danger to your very existence · extraordinary = beyond what is normal · legitimate = rightful and accepted

Chapter 20, Section I, “Media Echo Chambers, Negative Partisanship, and the Erosion of Democratic Trust.”

Reading JThe Constitutional Design Under Stress

The cumulative effect of partisan gerrymandering, media fragmentation, negative partisanship, and the other forces driving polarization has been to subject the Madisonian design to levels of institutional stress that previous generations would have found difficult to imagine.

The Senate filibuster, a procedural rule requiring a supermajority of sixty votes to advance most legislation, has been used with increasing frequency to prevent the majority from enacting significant legislation on contested issues, so that the minority can routinely veto the majority’s agenda. The confirmation process for executive branch appointees and federal judges has become a bitter partisan battle in which the norms of good-faith consideration and deference to presidential prerogative have been progressively eroded.

And the impeachment process, intended by the Framers as the ultimate constitutional check on executive misconduct, has been used with increasing frequency in ways that reflect partisan calculation rather than constitutional principle, diminishing its credibility as a mechanism of genuine accountability.

Word help: cumulative = built up over time · filibuster = a tactic that delays or blocks a vote in the Senate · supermajority = more than half, such as sixty of 100 · confirmation = Senate approval of a nominee · prerogative = a special right of an office · impeachment = formal charges against an official

Chapter 20, Section I, “The Constitutional Design Under Stress.”

Reading KWe Have Been Here Before

None of these developments necessarily represents a fatal threat to the republic; the constitutional system has survived comparable periods of partisan polarization before: the decades before the Civil War, the early twentieth century conflicts between Progressive Era reformers and the conservative Republican establishment, and the intense partisan conflicts of the Reconstruction era.

But each of those earlier periods was ultimately resolved through some combination of electoral realignment, social movement pressure, and institutional adaptation that restored a degree of productive functionality to the constitutional system. Whether the current polarization will be similarly resolved, and through what mechanisms, is one of the most consequential and most uncertain questions in contemporary American politics.

Word help: comparable = similar · Progressive Era = about 1890 to 1920, a time of reform · establishment = the group that holds the most power · electoral realignment = a lasting shift in which groups support which party · functionality = ability to work · consequential = very important

Chapter 20, Section I, “The Constitutional Design Under Stress.”

Algorithms and Fair Treatment

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 3: Evaluate the strategic risks and constitutional concerns posed by artificial intelligence in administrative governance and surveillance, with particular attention to how algorithmic decision-making challenges Fourth and Fifth Amendment protections and the democratic principle of transparency.

IN MY WORDS: What happens to fair treatment when a computer, and not a person, helps decide?

Reading LAI Enters Government

The integration of artificial intelligence into the operations of government, into law enforcement, social services administration, judicial decision-making, and national security surveillance, represents one of the most significant and least publicly understood transformations in the relationship between citizens and the state in the contemporary era.

AI-driven systems offer genuine potential benefits: greater consistency in decision-making, the identification of patterns invisible to human analysis, and more efficient allocation of public resources. But they also introduce constitutional risks that existing legal frameworks are poorly equipped to address, and they challenge fundamental principles of due process, equal protection, and democratic accountability.

Word help: artificial intelligence = computer systems that do tasks that usually need human thinking · integration = bringing one thing into another · contemporary = of today · consistency = treating similar cases the same way · allocation = dividing up and giving out · accountability = being answerable for your actions

Chapter 20, Section II, “The Digital Frontier: AI, Surveillance, and Privacy.”

Check 5. Which is one benefit of AI in government listed in Reading L?
A. It removes the need for due process

Write the letter of the best answer, then explain in one sentence how the reading shows it.

Reading MOpaque Algorithms and Due Process

The expansion of algorithmic decision-making into domains where government exercises power over individual liberty, criminal justice, immigration, public benefits, and child welfare, raises due process concerns that go to the heart of the constitutional guarantee of fair treatment before the law is applied.

The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments’ protections of procedural due process require, at their core, that individuals whose liberty or property interests are at stake have meaningful notice of the basis for government action and a meaningful opportunity to challenge it.

When government decisions are made through complex, opaque algorithmic systems, proprietary software whose internal logic is not publicly disclosed and whose operation cannot be fully examined even by technical experts, the ability of affected individuals to understand the basis for the action taken against them and to mount an effective challenge is severely compromised.

Word help: algorithmic = made by following a computer program’s steps · procedural due process = fair steps the government must follow · notice = being told what is happening · opaque = hard or impossible to see into · proprietary = owned by a company and kept private · compromised = weakened

Chapter 20, Section II, “Algorithmic Governance and the Due Process Challenge.”

What to look for: Follow the arrows from “Perception” through each step to “Behavior.” Ask yourself: at which step could a person see inside and challenge the result?

Reading NPredictive Policing and Algorithmic Bias

Predictive policing systems, algorithms that analyze crime data, demographic information, and other variables to generate predictions about where crimes are likely to occur or who is likely to commit them, raise the most acute constitutional concerns. These systems use historical crime data that may reflect the patterns of past discriminatory enforcement rather than the actual distribution of criminal activity across communities.

The result can be a self-reinforcing feedback loop: predictive algorithms direct more police attention toward minority communities, this additional presence generates more arrests in those communities, and those arrests are fed back into the training data that shapes future predictions. The outcome is racially disparate results through a technical mechanism that is not formally intentional but is structurally discriminatory.

This is an example of algorithmic bias: the potential for automated decision-making systems to reflect and amplify human prejudices.

Word help: predictive policing = using data to guess where crime may happen · acute = very serious · discriminatory = treating people unfairly because of a group they belong to · feedback loop = a cycle where results feed back and strengthen the cause · disparate = clearly unequal · algorithmic bias = a computer system repeating or increasing human prejudice

Chapter 20, Section II, “Algorithmic Governance and the Due Process Challenge.”

Visual FA Feedback Loop in Predictive Policing

Use this diagram with Reading N. It was made for this assignment to show the loop the chapter describes.

What to look for: Follow the arrows and find where the loop closes. Notice that no step has to be intentional for the loop to repeat.

Diagram made for this assignment from Chapter 20, Section II. It is an illustration, not a historical photograph.

Reading OBail, Sentencing, and State v. Loomis

The bail and sentencing algorithms examined in Chapter 10’s discussion of algorithmic justice present a parallel set of concerns. When a judge relies on a risk assessment score generated by a proprietary algorithm to determine whether to detain a defendant before trial or what sentence to impose, and when the defendant cannot access or examine the algorithm’s logic because it is a trade secret, the constitutional guarantee of a meaningful hearing, of the ability to confront and challenge the evidence used against you, is at minimum severely strained.

The Wisconsin Supreme Court’s decision in State v. Loomis (2016) upheld the use of such algorithms in sentencing while acknowledging the due process concerns they raised. But critics argued the decision failed to adequately grapple with what “meaningful challenge” actually requires when the challenger cannot examine the mechanism being challenged.

Word help: bail = money or a promise that lets a defendant wait outside jail before trial · detain = hold in custody · risk assessment = a score that estimates how likely something is · trade secret = business information a company keeps private · confront = face and answer · grapple = struggle to deal with

Chapter 20, Section II, “Algorithmic Governance and the Due Process Challenge.”

Part 5 of 9

Surveillance and Privacy

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 3: Evaluate the strategic risks and constitutional concerns posed by artificial intelligence in administrative governance and surveillance, with particular attention to how algorithmic decision-making challenges Fourth and Fifth Amendment protections and the democratic principle of transparency.

IN MY WORDS: How can the Fourth Amendment protect privacy when cameras and computers can watch everyone?

Reading PThe Fourth Amendment Frontier

The Fourth Amendment’s protection against unreasonable searches and seizures has been continuously tested by the expansion of government surveillance capabilities, from the wiretapping issues addressed in Katz v. United States to the cell phone location data at issue in Carpenter v. United States.

The development of AI-enhanced mass surveillance capabilities, systems capable of monitoring and analyzing the movements, communications, associations, and behaviors of entire populations simultaneously, represents the most extreme version of this challenge, one that strains the Fourth Amendment’s conceptual framework in ways that no previous surveillance technology has approached.

Word help: unreasonable searches and seizures = government searches or takings without good reason · surveillance = close watching · wiretapping = secretly listening to phone calls · location data = records of where a phone or person has been · AI-enhanced = made stronger with artificial intelligence · conceptual framework = the ideas a rule is built on

Chapter 20, Section II, “Mass Surveillance, Privacy, and the Fourth Amendment Frontier.”

Visual GThe Bill of Rights on Display

Use this picture with Reading P and Source C. It shows the Bill of Rights displayed behind glass.

What to look for: Read the carved words above the frame. Notice that the original document is protected behind glass.

Chapter 20, Figure 3, photograph reproduced in the chapter (the display of the Bill of Rights; no people are shown).

Source CThe Fourth Amendment

Ratified in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights, this amendment sets limits on government searches. This is a primary source, and it is in the public domain.

“The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.”

Word help: secure = safe from intrusion · persons, houses, papers, and effects = people, homes, documents, and belongings · warrant = a court order allowing a search · probable cause = good reasons to believe a crime or evidence is involved · oath or affirmation = a sworn promise to tell the truth · particularly describing = naming exactly

U.S. Constitution, Amendment IV (1791). Text checked at law.cornell.edu/constitution/fourth_amendment, which prints it in lower case. Primary source.

Source question. Use Source C. Pick two words or phrases that matter for facial recognition and explain how.

Reading QFacial Recognition and the Third-Party Doctrine

Facial recognition technology provides the clearest current example. When deployed in public spaces, in transportation hubs, shopping districts, political demonstrations, and streets, facial recognition systems can identify and track individuals without their knowledge or consent, creating comprehensive records of their movements, associations, and activities over time.

The legal question of whether this constitutes a “search” under the Fourth Amendment, and therefore whether it requires the individualized probable cause and judicial warrant that the Amendment’s core protections demand, has not been definitively resolved by the Supreme Court.

Under the third-party doctrine established in earlier cases, information that individuals expose in public spaces may not be entitled to Fourth Amendment protection. But as the Court suggested in Carpenter, the aggregation of comprehensive location and movement data over time may create a qualitatively different privacy interest than any individual piece of publicly observable information.

Word help: facial recognition = software that identifies people by their faces · consent = permission · individualized = about one specific person · judicial warrant = a judge’s order · third-party doctrine = the idea that information shared with others has weaker protection · aggregation = putting many small pieces together

Chapter 20, Section II, “Mass Surveillance, Privacy, and the Fourth Amendment Frontier.”

Check 6. What did the Court suggest in Carpenter about location data?
A. Public information never has any privacy interest
B. Gathering a lot of location data over time may create a different privacy interest than one piece of public information
C. Phones cannot be searched
D. Only the police can own phones
Write the letter of the best answer, then explain in one sentence how the reading shows it.

Reading RWhy It Matters: The Chilling Effect

The stakes of getting this constitutional question right are not merely theoretical. A government equipped with AI-enhanced mass surveillance capabilities and operating without meaningful constitutional constraints would have unprecedented power to monitor, identify, and respond to political dissent, civic organizing, and protest activities, precisely the forms of civic participation that the First Amendment’s protections of speech, assembly, and petition were designed to protect from government surveillance and deterrence.

The potential chilling effect of comprehensive government monitoring on the willingness of citizens to exercise their constitutional rights is one of the most serious threats to democratic self-governance that the AI era presents.

Word help: theoretical = only an idea, not real · constraints = limits · unprecedented = never seen before · dissent = disagreement with the government · deterrence = making people afraid to act · chilling effect = when fear of being watched stops people from using their rights

Chapter 20, Section II, “Mass Surveillance, Privacy, and the Fourth Amendment Frontier.”

Part 6 of 9

Disinformation and Legitimacy

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 4: Assess the impact of digital disinformation on the marketplace of ideas and the formation of public opinion, explaining how the deliberate spread of false information threatens institutional legitimacy and the quality of democratic self-governance.

IN MY WORDS: How can false information weaken trust in elections and institutions, and why is it hard for government to stop it?

Reading SWhat Is Disinformation?

Among the most consequential and most constitutionally complex challenges facing the American republic is the deliberate production and distribution of false information designed to undermine democratic governance. Disinformation, false information spread deliberately to deceive, is not a new phenomenon in American politics; the history of American political communication includes ample examples of deliberate falsehood deployed for partisan advantage.

What has changed in the digital era is the scale, speed, and targeting precision with which disinformation can be produced and distributed, and the difficulty of distinguishing deliberate disinformation from the ordinary errors and biases that characterize all political communication.

Word help: consequential = having big effects · constitutionally complex = hard to handle under constitutional rules · deliberate = done on purpose · falsehood = something untrue · partisan advantage = a gain for one political side · targeting precision = aiming at exactly the right people

Chapter 20, Section III, “Disinformation, the Information Environment, and Democratic Legitimacy.”

Check 7. Which fact makes disinformation different in the digital era, according to Reading S?
A. It is brand new
B. Its scale, speed, and targeting precision are greater
C. It is always true
D. It only appears in newspapers
Write the letter of the best answer, then explain in one sentence how the reading shows it.

Reading THow Disinformation Threatens Legitimacy

The threat that disinformation poses to institutional legitimacy operates through several channels. False information about electoral fraud can undermine public confidence in election results, making it difficult for citizens to accept the legitimacy of outcomes that the democratic process has produced.

Disinformation about government institutions, about the competence or loyalty of public health agencies, law enforcement agencies, or national security institutions, can erode the public trust that makes those institutions capable of performing their functions.

And the deliberate amplification of social divisions through disinformation designed to make partisan opponents appear threatening or alien can contribute to the negative partisanship and erosion of democratic trust that feed the broader polarization crisis.

Word help: institutional legitimacy = how much people see an institution as rightful and worth trusting and obeying · electoral fraud = cheating in an election · undermine = weaken · erode = wear away · amplification = making louder or bigger · alien = foreign or strange

Chapter 20, Section III, “Disinformation, the Information Environment, and Democratic Legitimacy.”

Reading UThe First Amendment Problem

The constitutional challenge of addressing disinformation is severe, because the First Amendment’s protection of freedom of speech and press applies to false political statements as well as true ones. The Supreme Court’s decision in United States v. Alvarez (2012), which struck down a federal law criminalizing false claims of military honor, strongly suggested that the government cannot generally regulate political falsehood through criminal law, since the remedy the Constitution contemplates for false speech is more speech rather than enforced silence.

This constraint does not entirely foreclose governmental response. Disclosures, corrections, labeling requirements, and regulation of foreign-government-funded political communication may all be constitutionally available. But the most powerful tools lie not with government regulation but with platform governance, media literacy education, and the development of institutional and social norms that treat the deliberate spread of political falsehood as a form of democratic corruption rather than protected political competition.

Word help: criminalizing = making something a crime · contemplates = has in mind · foreclose = rule out completely · disclosures = required public statements of facts · labeling requirements = rules to mark content with a label · platform governance = rules that online companies set for their sites · media literacy = skill in judging media · norms = shared expectations of behavior

Chapter 20, Section III, “Disinformation, the Information Environment, and Democratic Legitimacy.”

Part 7 of 9

Electoral Reform Proposals

CORE OBJECTIVE

FQ 5: Compare various structural reform proposals — including ranked-choice voting, Electoral College reform, congressional term limits, and Supreme Court reform — evaluating the democratic rationale, constitutional feasibility, and likely consequences of each.

IN MY WORDS: What would ranked-choice voting and Electoral College changes do, and what are the arguments on each side?

Reading VJudging Reform Proposals

The challenges of polarization, algorithmic governance, and digital disinformation have generated a substantial and growing body of proposed reforms to the electoral system, the institutions of government, and the constitutional framework itself.

Evaluating these proposals requires applying several distinct standards at once: empirical analysis of whether the reform would produce its claimed benefits; constitutional analysis of whether it is legally feasible without a constitutional amendment; political analysis of whether enough consensus exists to enact it; and democratic theory analysis of whether its likely consequences fit the core values of democratic self-government.

Word help: proposed reforms = suggested changes · empirical = based on evidence you can measure · feasible = possible to do · consensus = wide agreement · democratic theory = ideas about what makes a democracy fair · framework = basic structure

Chapter 20, Section III, “Strengthening the ‘Structural Equilibrium’: Reform Proposals.”

Reading WRanked-Choice Voting

Ranked-choice voting, an electoral system in which voters rank candidates in order of preference rather than selecting a single candidate, has been adopted by a growing number of jurisdictions in the United States, including Maine (which uses it for statewide and federal elections), Alaska, and many cities, and has been proposed as a reform at the federal level.

The most frequently cited benefit is the elimination of the “spoiler” effect, in which a third-party candidate who draws votes away from the major-party candidate ideologically closest to them can cause that candidate to lose to the more distant one. Under ranked-choice voting, voters can rank a third-party candidate first without fear of wasting their vote, because if that candidate is eliminated in the first round, the votes are redistributed to the voters’ second choices.

A second claimed benefit is the reduction of negative campaigning and extreme partisanship. Under a plurality system, a candidate who energizes their base through polarizing rhetoric while repelling moderate voters can still win; under ranked-choice voting, a candidate with intense enthusiasm among a plurality but strong negative reactions from a majority is more likely to lose, because those voters’ later rankings consolidate against them.

Word help: ranked-choice voting = voters rank candidates 1st, 2nd, 3rd; if no one has a majority, last place is dropped and votes move to next choices · jurisdictions = places with their own government · spoiler = a minor candidate who splits a side’s votes · plurality = the most votes, even if not a majority · base = a candidate’s core supporters · consolidate = join together

Chapter 20, Section III, “Electoral Reforms: Ranked-Choice Voting and the Electoral College.”

Reading XWhat Critics Say About Ranked-Choice Voting

The chapter lists the benefits that supporters claim for ranked-choice voting. Critics make arguments of their own. Some ask why winning with a plurality but not a majority should be seen as a problem at all.

Critics also point to exhausted ballots: if a voter ranks only one candidate and that candidate is eliminated, the ballot may not count in later rounds. Some say this gives voters who rank every candidate more voting power than voters who rank only one.

Others worry about complexity and voter confusion, and about whether voters will be properly educated about the new system, which could lead to incomplete ballots.

Word help: plurality = the most votes, even if under 50 percent · exhausted ballot = a ballot with no ranked candidates left in the count · power = the weight a vote has · complexity = being complicated · incomplete = not fully filled in · critics = people who disagree with something

Added for this assignment to balance Reading W. Summary of arguments reported by the National Conference of State Legislatures, “Ranked Choice Voting” (ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/ranked-choice-voting).

Check 8. Which is an argument critics make against ranked-choice voting?
A. It always makes elections faster
B. Ballots can be exhausted if the voter’s ranked candidates are all eliminated
C. It cannot be used in cities
D. It removes all third parties
Write the letter of the best answer, then explain in one sentence how the reading shows it.

Reading YThe Electoral College: The Case Against

The Electoral College represents a different kind of electoral reform debate, one involving a constitutional provision that cannot be changed without the arduous process of constitutional amendment, though the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact offers a potential workaround.

Critics of the Electoral College argue that the winner-take-all system in most states systematically concentrates presidential campaign activity in a small number of battleground states while voters in safely partisan states are effectively disenfranchised: their votes contribute to an inevitable outcome rather than determining a contested result.

They also note that the allocation of electoral votes on the basis of total congressional delegation, including senators, means that voters in small states have mathematically greater per-capita electoral weight than voters in large states, creating a systematic departure from the democratic principle of equal voting power.

Word help: Electoral College = the system of electors who formally choose the President · arduous = very hard · interstate compact = an agreement among states · workaround = a way to get around a problem · battleground state = a state where the vote is close · per-capita = per person

Chapter 20, Section III, “Electoral Reforms: Ranked-Choice Voting and the Electoral College.”

Reading ZThe Electoral College: The Case For

Defenders of the Electoral College respond that the geographic distribution requirement it imposes, forcing candidates to build coalitions that are sustainable across diverse regions rather than simply maximizing urban or coastal population centers, is a feature rather than a bug, producing a form of coalition-building that a pure national popular vote might not.

They also note that the Electoral College has produced clear, definitive outcomes in the overwhelming majority of elections, avoiding the recounts, runoffs, and contested results that might accompany a close national popular vote.

Word help: defenders = people who support something · geographic distribution = spread across places · sustainable = able to last · feature rather than a bug = a good part of the design, not a mistake · definitive = clear and final · runoff = an extra election between top candidates

Chapter 20, Section III, “Electoral Reforms: Ranked-Choice Voting and the Electoral College.”

Part 8 of 9

Term Limits, Courts, and a Living Framework

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 5: Compare various structural reform proposals — including ranked-choice voting, Electoral College reform, congressional term limits, and Supreme Court reform — evaluating the democratic rationale, constitutional feasibility, and likely consequences of each.

FQ 6: Identify the ways in which the Constitution remains a living document capable of managing twenty-first century conflicts, explaining how the Framers' design of institutional friction and adaptability has enabled the republic to survive previous periods of acute stress.

IN MY WORDS: What are the arguments for and against term limits and Supreme Court terms, and how does the Constitution allow change?

Reading AAThe Case for Term Limits

Term limits, restrictions on the number of terms individuals may serve in a specific office, have been proposed for members of Congress and for federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, as responses to what reformers characterize as the excessive entrenchment of institutional power in the hands of individuals who serve for decades without meaningful democratic accountability.

The case for term limits rests on several premises: that career politicians develop an orientation toward self-preservation and institutional power that displaces genuine policy service; that long-serving members of Congress accumulate leverage through committee seniority that insulates their states and districts from national electoral trends; and that the indefinite tenure of Supreme Court justices has transformed judicial nominations into high-stakes battles whose intensity is disproportionate to the actual governance implications of any single appointment.

Word help: term limits = a cap on how many terms someone can serve · entrenchment = being firmly and permanently in place · premises = starting beliefs an argument rests on · self-preservation = protecting yourself · seniority = rank from long service · insulates = protects · tenure = time in office

Chapter 20, Section III, “Institutional Reforms: Term Limits, Court Reform, and the Redistricting Problem.”

Reading ABThe Constitutional Barrier

The constitutional barriers to term limits for federal officeholders are significant. The Supreme Court held in U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton (1995) that states cannot impose term limits on their congressional delegations through state law, because the qualifications for federal office are established by the Constitution itself and cannot be supplemented by state action.

Congressional term limits therefore require a constitutional amendment, which itself requires two-thirds majorities in both houses of Congress, whose members would be voting to limit their own tenure, and ratification by three-quarters of state legislatures. This procedural barrier is formidable but not theoretically insuperable; it simply means that the political support required for term limits must be sufficiently broad and durable to survive the amendment process.

Word help: delegation = the group of lawmakers a state sends · qualifications = the requirements to hold an office · supplemented = added to · ratification = formal approval · formidable = very hard to overcome · insuperable = impossible to overcome · durable = lasting

Chapter 20, Section III, “Institutional Reforms: Term Limits, Court Reform, and the Redistricting Problem.”

Check 9. Why can a state not set term limits for its members of Congress, according to U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton?
A. States have no elections
B. The Constitution sets the qualifications for federal office and states cannot add to them
C. Congress has no members
D. The Court never decides such cases
Write the letter of the best answer, then explain in one sentence how the reading shows it.

Reading ACThe Case Against Term Limits

The critics of congressional term limits raise substantive governance concerns beyond the procedural barriers. Long-serving members of Congress develop policy expertise, institutional knowledge, and relationships with executive branch officials and foreign counterparts that take years to develop and that are genuinely valuable to effective governance.

If term limits reduce the average tenure of congressional members, the primary beneficiaries of that expertise vacuum may not be the voters but the permanent bureaucracy, the lobbying community, and the executive branch, all of whom interact with Congress continuously and whose institutional memories will outlast any wave of term-limited newcomers.

Word help: substantive = about real substance, not just procedure · institutional knowledge = what people learn from long experience in an organization · counterparts = people in a similar role · expertise vacuum = a gap left when experienced people leave · bureaucracy = the government’s agencies and staff · lobbying community = people paid to influence lawmakers

Chapter 20, Section III, “Institutional Reforms: Term Limits, Court Reform, and the Redistricting Problem.”

Reading ADEighteen-Year Terms for Justices

Supreme Court reform, specifically the proposal to impose eighteen-year staggered terms on justices rather than the current lifetime appointment, has gained particular attention as the Court has become an increasingly consequential battlefield for social and economic policy.

Proponents argue that lifetime tenure was designed for an era of shorter life expectancy and less consequential judicial power, and that the current system creates strong incentives for presidents and senators to treat confirmation battles as existential political contests, since a single appointment can shift the Court’s ideological balance for decades. Staggered eighteen-year terms would ensure that each president has a predictable opportunity to appoint justices without depending on the strategic timing of retirements or deaths, reducing the high-stakes character of individual appointments.

The chapter reports the proponents’ case. The question below asks you to think about what opponents might say.

Word help: staggered = spread out so they end at different times · lifetime appointment = serving until death or retirement · proponents = supporters of a proposal · incentive = a reason to act · ideological balance = the mix of political views on a court · predictable = able to be known ahead of time

Chapter 20, Section III, “Institutional Reforms: Term Limits, Court Reform, and the Redistricting Problem.” The last paragraph is a short note added for this assignment.

Visual JFive Reform Proposals Compared

Use this chart with Readings AA through AD. It was made for this assignment from the chapter’s reform discussion.

Made for this assignment from Chapter 20, Section III. “How it could be adopted” follows the chapter; where the chapter is silent, the cell says so.

Compare and think. Use Visual J. Which reform in the chart faces the highest constitutional barrier, and which the lowest? For the Supreme Court terms proposal, name one argument a supporter makes (Reading AD) and one objection you think an opponent might raise.

Reading AEAdaptive Architecture

One of the most persistent misconceptions about the American Constitution is that the Framers produced a static blueprint. The historical record suggests a more nuanced understanding: the Framers were deeply aware that a constitution designed for a republic of four million citizens in 1787 would need to adapt as the republic grew and changed, and they built mechanisms of adaptation into the document’s structure.

The amendment process, deliberately demanding but not impossibly difficult, requires broad consensus, preventing momentary majorities from rewriting fundamental law while allowing sustained national consensus to update it. The vesting of interpretive authority in the federal judiciary created a way to adapt principles to new circumstances through authoritative interpretation.

And the broad language of many provisions, the “unreasonable searches and seizures” of the Fourth Amendment, the “due process of law” of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, the “necessary and proper” powers of Congress, reflects a deliberate choice to state principles that can apply to unanticipated circumstances rather than rules calibrated to 1787 conditions.

Word help: misconception = a wrong idea people commonly hold · static blueprint = a plan that never changes · nuanced = more careful and detailed · momentary majority = a majority that exists only briefly · vesting = giving a power to · calibrated = set exactly for

Chapter 20, Section IV, “The Framers’ Design as Adaptive Architecture.”

Source DHow to Amend the Constitution

Article V of the Constitution, written in 1787, sets out the ways to propose and approve amendments. This is a primary source, and it is in the public domain.

“The Congress, whenever two thirds of both houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose amendments to this Constitution,”
“or, on the application of the legislatures of two thirds of the several states, shall call a convention for proposing amendments,”
“when ratified by the legislatures of three fourths of the several states, or by conventions in three fourths thereof”

Word help: amendments = formal changes · deem it necessary = decide it is needed · application = a formal request · convention = a special meeting · ratified = approved · legislatures = lawmaking bodies

U.S. Constitution, Article V (1787). Quotations (in the lower case used by the source) checked at law.cornell.edu/constitution/articlev; the Constitution’s own Article V is longer. Primary source.

Reading AFThe Same Words, a New Meaning

The constitutional framework’s adaptability has been most visibly demonstrated in its response to the civil rights crisis of the twentieth century. The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868 to address the specific injustice of post-Civil War racial subordination, became in the twentieth century the constitutional foundation for the protection of individual rights against state action across a much broader range of circumstances than its immediate context.

That transformation was achieved through the combination of constitutional litigation, legislative action, and the sustained pressure of social movements. The same document that was used to justify racial segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson was used to dismantle it in Brown v. Board of Education, not because the text changed but because the nation’s understanding of what equal protection required evolved through the democratic and judicial processes the Constitution created.

Word help: adaptability = ability to change for new conditions · subordination = being treated as lower in rank · ratified = formally approved · litigation = taking cases to court · segregation = forced separation of races · dismantle = take apart · equal protection = the rule that the law must treat people equally

Part 9 of 9

Make Your Argument

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 1: How can the American constitutional framework adapt to the strategic challenges of the twenty-first century while maintaining institutional legitimacy?

FQ 6: Identify the ways in which the Constitution remains a living document capable of managing twenty-first century conflicts, explaining how the Framers' design of institutional friction and adaptability has enabled the republic to survive previous periods of acute stress.

IN MY WORDS: What keeps people trusting the Constitution, and what could wear that trust away?

Reading AGInstitutional Legitimacy: The Thread That Connects

The concept of institutional legitimacy, the degree to which a government’s institutions and procedures are seen as authoritative and worthy of public trust and compliance, is the thread that connects every topic this chapter has examined.

Political polarization is a threat to institutional legitimacy because it undermines the social trust that makes citizens willing to accept political outcomes they disagree with. Algorithmic governance threatens legitimacy when it makes the bases of government action opaque and unchallengeable. Disinformation threatens legitimacy when it persuades citizens that electoral results are fraudulent, that institutions are corrupt, or that the democratic process is systematically rigged against them.

And the reform proposals examined in this chapter are valuable precisely to the extent that they restore or strengthen the institutional legitimacy that makes democratic self-governance possible.

Word help: institutional legitimacy = how much people see government’s institutions as rightful, trustworthy, and worth obeying · authoritative = having rightful power · compliance = obeying · opaque = hard to see into · unchallengeable = impossible to question · rigged = set up unfairly in advance

Chapter 20, Section IV, “Institutional Legitimacy and the Stakes of Reform.”

Reading AHEssential and Fragile

The most important insight that the study of American government provides about institutional legitimacy is that it is simultaneously the most essential and the most fragile resource in a democratic system. Essential, because a government whose institutions lack legitimacy cannot effectively govern: it can compel compliance through force, but it cannot achieve the voluntary cooperation that makes democratic governance both effective and self-sustaining.

Fragile, because legitimacy is built slowly through consistent, fair, and transparent institutional performance, and can be destroyed far more rapidly than it can be built, by a single catastrophic failure of institutional integrity, by sustained patterns of perceived bias or corruption, or by the relentless erosion of public confidence that disinformation and hyper-partisanship can produce.

The American republic has survived crises of institutional legitimacy before, the Civil War, the Watergate scandal, and the contested election of 2000, through institutional resilience, democratic renewal, and the willingness of citizens to keep engaging with the constitutional system as a legitimate framework even when they deeply disagreed with specific outcomes.

Word help: insight = a clear understanding · compel = force · voluntary = by choice · self-sustaining = able to keep itself going · integrity = honesty and soundness · erosion = slow wearing away · renewal = making something fresh again

Chapter 20, Section IV, “Institutional Legitimacy and the Stakes of Reform.”

Check 10. Why does the chapter call institutional legitimacy fragile?
A. It cannot be seen
B. It is built slowly but can be destroyed much faster
C. It exists only in wartime
D. It belongs only to the courts
Write the letter of the best answer, then explain in one sentence how the reading shows it.

Reading AIChapter Conclusion

This textbook has traced the full arc of the American constitutional system, from the philosophical foundations in the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, through the institutional architecture of separated powers, federalism, and rights protection, to the policy domains of economic security, social welfare, and foreign affairs, and finally to the civic culture and political dynamics that animate the system from the bottom up.

The essential question of this chapter, how the framework can adapt to the strategic challenges of the twenty-first century while maintaining institutional legitimacy, does not have a simple answer. The specific reforms examined here, ranked-choice voting, Electoral College modification, term limits, and court restructuring, each involve genuine trade-offs between competing democratic values, and each is constrained by constitutional provisions, political realities, and empirical uncertainties.

What can be said with more confidence is that the constitutional system of separated powers, federalism, individual rights, and democratic accountability has demonstrated a remarkable capacity for adaptation over two and a half centuries.

Franklin’s question about the rising or setting sun has been answered, imperfectly and provisionally, by more than two centuries of history. Whether the sun continues to rise depends on the quality of American political leadership, the health of American civic culture, the resilience of American democratic institutions, and the willingness of American citizens to engage with the hard, patient, imperfect work of self-governance. The republic’s future now depends, in part, on what you do with the tools this textbook has given you.

Word help: arc = the whole path from start to end · architecture = the way something is built · animate = give life to · trade-offs = giving up one good thing to get another · empirical = based on evidence · provisionally = for now, not final · resilience = ability to recover

Chapter 20, Chapter Conclusion.

Source EMadison on Controlling Government

James Madison wrote this in Federalist No. 51 in 1788, explaining why the new Constitution needed more than elections to control government. This passage is the one the chapter uses for its Primary Source question. This is a primary source, and it is in the public domain.

“If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary.”
“In framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself.”
“A dependence on the people is, no doubt, the primary control on the government; but experience has taught mankind the necessity of auxiliary precautions.”

Word help: external controls = limits from outside the government · internal controls = limits built inside the government · administered = managed · the governed = the people who are ruled · oblige = require · auxiliary precautions = extra safeguards

James Madison, Federalist No. 51 (1788). Quotations checked word for word at avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/fed51.asp. Primary source.
